% =====================================================================
\section{Motivation}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Why Bayesian inference for a trading agent?}
A fixed-budget investor in a liquid ETF must, each day, choose
$a_t \in \{\text{short}, \text{flat}, \text{long}\}$ under
low signal-to-noise and transaction frictions.

\medskip
Three statistical questions arise -- all classically Bayesian:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \alert{How confident are we in each action's value?} A point
        estimate of $Q(s,a)$ is uninformative when per-cell data is
        sparse.
  \item \alert{How should we explore?} $\varepsilon$-greedy uses a
        tuning parameter independent of what we already know.
  \item \alert{How should we borrow strength?} The state space contains
        rare tail regimes; hierarchical priors are the textbook tool.
\end{itemize}
\note{Open with the framing: this is not an RL paper, it is a Bayesian
inference paper that happens to make trading decisions. The three
questions are the three Bayesian moves we will make. Linger on
``the prior buys you something'' as the through-line.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{What classical Q-learning leaves on the table}
\textbf{Tabular $\varepsilon$-greedy Q-learning} updates point estimates
\begin{equation*}
Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha\!\left[\,r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') \,-\, Q(s,a)\right].
\end{equation*}
What it gives back: a single number per $(s,a)$ cell.

\medskip
What's missing:
\begin{itemize}
  \item No \alert{uncertainty} over $Q(s,a)$ -- so no principled
        exploration, no calibrated decision under risk.
  \item Hyper-sensitive to $\alpha_t$ and $\varepsilon_t$ schedules.
  \item No way to \alert{borrow strength} across actions or states.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
We will replace this with a generative model, a posterior, and a
decision rule derived from that posterior.
\note{Don't trash classical Q-learning -- it's our baseline and it does
well here. The point is just that it returns one number where we want
a distribution. Use the word ``calibrated'' explicitly; it foreshadows
the validity check in nb 09.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{MDP setup}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{The decision process}
We work with a discrete-time controlled process
$\mathcal{M} = (\St, \A, P, R, \gamma, H)$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{State} $s_t$ -- continuous feature vector
        $x_{s_t} \in \R^p$ from SPY's own price history (causal).
  \item \textbf{Action} $a_t \in \A = \{-1, 0, +1\}$ (short, flat,
        long).
  \item \textbf{Reward}
        $R_t = a_t \cdot r_{t+1} - c_t\,|a_t - a_{t-1}|$,
        \quad $r_{t+1} = \log(P_{t+1}/P_t)$.
  \item \textbf{Volatility-dependent cost}
        $c_t = c_0 + \lambda \cdot \widehat\sigma_t^{(20)}$,
        with $c_0 = 5$bps, $\lambda = 0.5$.
  \item \textbf{Discount} $\gamma = 0.95$; horizon $H = 60$ trading
        days.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
\alert{Price-taker assumption:}
$P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t, a_t) \approx P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t)$ -- a small retail
trade does not move the market.
\note{Spend ~30 seconds on each of state / action / reward. Call out the
vol-dependent cost as a deliberate modelling choice -- a constant cost
hides the fact that spreads widen in turbulence. Stationarity
assumption is the honest caveat; we will come back to it.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{The key methodological move}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Where the previous draft went wrong}
The first version of this project used the \emph{TD-bootstrapped target}
as the observation:
\begin{equation*}
\tilde y_t = r_t + \gamma \max_{a'} \widehat Q(s_{t+1}, a').
\end{equation*}
This is what Dearden, Friedman \& Russell (1998) do. It is \alert{not a
coherent generative model} -- $\tilde y_t$ depends on the estimator
$\widehat Q$ itself.

\bigskip
\textbf{Revised model.} Each observation is a finite-horizon
\emph{Monte Carlo} return collected under a fixed behavior policy:
\begin{equation}
\boxed{\;y_t \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{H} \gamma^k R_{t+k}.\;}
\end{equation}
A real number, computable from the data alone. Now we have a real
likelihood.
\note{This is the methodological centrepiece of the talk -- the move
from bootstrapped TD to MC returns. Audience will include the
professor and graders who care about this distinction. Be explicit:
``the previous draft was wrong; this is why''. Don't rush.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Features and MC-return targets}
\begin{columns}[T]
  \begin{column}{0.45\textwidth}
    \textbf{State features}
    ($x_s \in \R^4$, strictly causal):
    \begin{itemize}\small
      \item $x_1$: 5-day momentum,
            $z$-scored over trailing 252 days.
      \item $x_2$: log of 20-day realised vol, centred over 252 days.
      \item $x_3$: $(P_t - \mathrm{MA}_{200,t})/\mathrm{MA}_{200,t}$.
      \item $x_4 = 1$ (intercept).
    \end{itemize}
    \medskip
    \textbf{Pre-1994 window} is reserved for prior hyperparameter
    elicitation and never touched again.
  \end{column}
  \begin{column}{0.55\textwidth}
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_mc_targets}
    \small Distribution of $y_t$ by behaviour-policy action, training
    window.
  \end{column}
\end{columns}
\note{Two ideas: (1) features are 4-dim and causal, (2) the histogram
shows $y_t$ has plenty of dispersion -- enough signal for the
regression to do work. The pre-94 window is a fairness move; mention
that no part of the test set ever leaks into the prior.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Bayesian model}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Likelihood: Bayesian linear regression on MC returns}
For each transition with $(s_t, a_t) = (s, a)$:
\begin{equation*}
\boxed{\;y_t \;\big|\; x_{s_t},\,a_t = a,\,\bm{\beta}_a,\,\sigma^2
\;\sim\; \N\!\big(x_{s_t}^\top \bm{\beta}_a,\; \sigma^2\big).\;}
\end{equation*}

\medskip
A per-action coefficient vector $\bm{\beta}_a \in \R^p$ and a shared
homoscedastic noise scale $\sigma^2$. The implied action-value function
is
\begin{equation*}
\widehat Q(s, a) \;=\; \E[y_t \mid x_s, a] \;=\; x_s^\top \bm{\beta}_a.
\end{equation*}

\medskip
\alert{Why linear?} Three reasons: interpretability, conjugate Gibbs
blocks, and the asymptotic agnostic ``one-step Newton'' reading. Richer
function classes (GP, BNN) are the natural follow-up.
\note{The whole RL problem has now collapsed to a Bayesian linear
regression. Three action-specific coefficient vectors, one noise scale.
Emphasise: ``This is what is in Gelman, chapter 14.'' That framing
matters for the audience.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Hierarchical prior: partial pooling across actions}
A naive independent-prior choice precludes borrowing strength. Instead
we put a multivariate-normal hierarchy:
\begin{align}
\bm{\beta}_a \mid \bm{\mu}_\beta, \bm{\Sigma}_\beta &\;\sim\;
\N\!\big(\bm{\mu}_\beta,\; \bm{\Sigma}_\beta\big),\quad a \in \A,\\
\bm{\mu}_\beta &\;\sim\; \N(\bm 0, \tau_0^2 I_p), \\
\bm{\Sigma}_\beta &\;\sim\; \IW(\nu_0, \bm\Lambda_0), \\
\sigma^2 &\;\sim\; \IG(a_0, b_0).
\end{align}

\medskip
With three actions, $\bm\mu_\beta$ is the \emph{cross-action mean}, and
each $\bm\beta_a$ is shrunk toward it. The textbook Gelman partial-pooling
story -- transplanted to RL.
\note{Spell out partial pooling: ``If $\mu_\beta$ were fixed, every
$\beta_a$ would be shrunk toward zero. Because $\mu_\beta$ is learned
from data, it is shrunk toward the cross-action average.'' This is the
Bayesian advantage at small $n_a$. Don't get bogged down in IW math;
move on.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Conjugate full conditionals -- exact Gibbs}
Let $X_a, \bm y_a$ stack the rows where $a_t = a$. Every full
conditional is closed form:

\begin{align*}
\bm\beta_a \mid \cdot &\;\sim\; \N(\bm m_a, V_a), \\
V_a^{-1} &= \sigma^{-2} X_a^\top X_a + \bm\Sigma_\beta^{-1}, \\
\bm m_a &= V_a\!\left(\sigma^{-2} X_a^\top \bm y_a + \bm\Sigma_\beta^{-1}\bm\mu_\beta\right).
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
\bm\mu_\beta \mid \cdot &\;\sim\; \N\!\big(\bm m_\mu, V_\mu\big), \quad
\bm\Sigma_\beta \mid \cdot \;\sim\; \IW\!\big(\nu_0 + |\A|, \bm\Lambda_0 + S\big), \\
\sigma^2 \mid \cdot &\;\sim\; \IG\!\big(a_0 + \tfrac{n}{2},\; b_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}\textstyle\sum_t (y_t - x_{s_t}^\top \bm\beta_{a_t})^2 \big).
\end{align*}

\medskip
\alert{Gibbs sweep cost:} $O(n p^2 + |\A| p^3)$. Production budget:
$4$ chains $\times 6000$ draws after $2000$ burn-in, runs in
$\sim 25$ s on a laptop.
\note{Reassure the audience: ``this is all standard conjugate stuff.'' The
non-obvious bit is that $\beta_a$ pools through $\Sigma_\beta$ -- not
through a hard tie. Skip past the IW formula if running short on time;
the point is ``exact Gibbs, no PPL''.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Student-$t$ extension via scale mixture}
Daily returns have heavy tails -- the Gaussian likelihood may
under-cover. The robust alternative:
\begin{equation*}
y_t \mid x_{s_t}, a_t, \bm\beta_a, \sigma^2, \nu \;\sim\; t_\nu\!\big(x_{s_t}^\top \bm\beta_a,\; \sigma^2\big),
\end{equation*}
implemented as a Gaussian scale mixture
\begin{equation*}
y_t \mid \lambda_t \sim \N(x_{s_t}^\top \bm\beta_a, \sigma^2/\lambda_t), \qquad
\lambda_t \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\nu/2, \nu/2).
\end{equation*}

\medskip
$\lambda_t$'s full conditional is Gamma; $\nu$ is updated by a
Metropolis-within-Gibbs step on $\log\nu$. Acceptance held inside
$[0.20, 0.45]$ per chain.

\medskip
\alert{Headline:} the Student-$t$ posterior is empirically
indistinguishable from the Gaussian on this dataset (see nb 06 /
robustness slide).
\note{Mention this only briefly. The robustness slide later carries
the empirical reading. The point of this slide is just ``we offered a
heavy-tail alternative, and the conjugate skeleton survives.''}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Decision rule}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Thompson sampling: posterior \emph{is} the policy}
At deployment time $t$, draw one joint posterior sample
$\tilde\theta = (\tilde{\bm\beta}_{-1}, \tilde{\bm\beta}_0, \tilde{\bm\beta}_{+1}) \sim p(\theta \mid \D)$,
then play
\begin{equation*}
\boxed{\;a_t \;=\; \arg\max_{a \in \A}\; x_{s_t}^\top \tilde{\bm\beta}_a.\;}
\end{equation*}

\medskip
What this gives us:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \alert{No $\varepsilon$ hyperparameter} -- exploration is
        driven by posterior width, not a tuning knob.
  \item \alert{Self-regulating}: as $\Var(\bm\beta_a \mid \D)$
        contracts, the policy automatically commits.
  \item Equivalent to PSRL (Osband, Russo, Van Roy 2013) for the
        contextual-bandit-with-MC-returns case.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
\textbf{Cadence:} one posterior draw \emph{per episode} (the full test
window). Justified empirically against per-step and monthly cadences
in nb 07.
\note{Two big claims to land here. First: ``the posterior IS the
exploration strategy'' -- no $\varepsilon$ to tune. Second: the
cadence choice (per-episode) is not arbitrary; nb 07 showed
per-step Thompson collapses to Sharpe $-4.6$ and trades 3.6x as
often. We picked the cadence empirically.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{What the posterior over $Q(s,a)$ looks like}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.78\linewidth]{fig_q_posterior}

\medskip
\small One mid-test state $x_s$, three actions, posterior of
$Q(s,a) = x_s^\top \bm\beta_a$. Thompson sampling picks the action
with the highest single draw from this joint posterior -- not the
posterior mean.
\note{Walk through what the figure says: ``three colored densities,
three actions, $Q$ on the x-axis, density on the y-axis. The width of
each density is the uncertainty; the gap between them is the signal.
Thompson sampling integrates over both.'' This is the
``calibrated decision under uncertainty'' slide.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Data and design}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Dataset: SPY, 1994--2026}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{fig_data_overview}

\medskip
\small
\textbf{Pre-train} 1993 (prior elicitation only) $\;|\;$
\textbf{Train} 1994-01 -- 2019-12 (6\,546 days, $\sim$6\,500 MC targets) $\;|\;$
\textbf{Test} 2020-04 -- 2026-04 (1\,589 days, includes COVID crash,
2022 bear, 2023--24 rally).
\note{Why this test window: it's deliberately stress-rich. If the
methods agreed only on a flat bull market, the comparison would not
be meaningful. The 2020--2026 regime is hostile to any
linear-feature three-action policy class.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Comparison design -- what's fair, what isn't}
\textbf{Three methods, one environment.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{(B) Bayesian Q (Thompson)} -- the proposed method.
  \item \textbf{(C1) Tabular $\varepsilon$-greedy} -- features
        quantile-binned; classic.
  \item \textbf{(C2) Linear FQI + $\varepsilon$-greedy} -- same linear
        features as B; isolates ``prior/posterior'' from ``linear
        features''.
  \item \textbf{Random} -- the laugh-test floor.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
\textbf{Fairness controls.}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Same data, same features, same reward, same cost model, same
        $\gamma$, same train/test split.
  \item C1, C2 grid-tuned on training; B uses fixed weakly-informative
        hyperparameters -- \alert{any Bayesian win is conservative}.
  \item All distributions reported are 95\% intervals over the
        relevant ensemble (posterior draws for B, seeds for C1/C2).
\end{itemize}
\note{The C2 baseline is the most important fairness move: it shares
linear features with B, so any gap between them is attributable to
the prior/posterior, not to the function class. Be ready for ``why
not RBF?'' -- the answer is conjugacy.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Evaluation: posterior-predictive throughout}
\textbf{No point estimates, ever.} Every reported quantity is a
\emph{distribution}.

\medskip
For each posterior draw $\theta^{(m)} \sim p(\theta \mid \D)$,
$m = 1, \dots, 500$:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Roll deterministic policy
        $\pi^{(m)}(s) = \arg\max_a x_s^\top \bm\beta_a^{(m)}$ on the
        test window.
  \item Compute Sharpe$^{(m)}$, MDD$^{(m)}$, Turnover$^{(m)}$.
  \item Report the full empirical distribution (mean and 95\% CrI).
\end{enumerate}

\medskip
For C1, C2: the analog ensemble is over $20$ optimisation seeds.
\textbf{Same ensemble width, same interval semantics.}

\medskip
\alert{Plus} a posterior-predictive calibration check: empirical 95\%
coverage of $y_t \in [q_{2.5}^{(m)}, q_{97.5}^{(m)}]$ on the test set.
\note{The line to deliver: ``Sharpe is a distribution.'' If anything is
the methodological signature of the talk, it's that. Drive it home --
the audience expects a single Sharpe number, and we are deliberately
refusing to give one.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Robustness}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Robustness -- Gaussian vs Student-$t$ likelihood}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{fig_student_t}

\medskip
\small Three rows, three metrics, three rows in each: Gaussian
Bayesian, Student-$t$ Bayesian, Linear FQI. Intervals overlap
everywhere. The Gaussian likelihood is enough; the heavy-tailed
variant doesn't change the conclusion.
\note{Two takeaways: (1) the Gaussian assumption is empirically
defensible on this MC-aggregated target ($y_t$ is a 60-day discounted
sum, central limit kicks in); (2) the framework is flexible enough to
swap in Student-$t$ with no change to the conjugate skeleton.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Validity check -- the calibration claim has teeth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth]{fig_prior_invariance}

\medskip
\small Three rows = three $\sigma^2$-prior strengths ($\nu_\sigma \in
\{0.1, 1.0, 4.0\}$, three orders of magnitude). Bars are
\alert{visually indistinguishable}. Sensitivity score
$\mathbf{0.000}$ on every metric.

\medskip
The $\sim$6\,500-row likelihood dominates four prior pseudo-observations
by three orders of magnitude -- exactly what calibrated Bayesian
inference looks like.
\note{This is the slide that turns ``calibrated uncertainty'' from
rhetoric into evidence. Bernstein--von Mises says the credible
intervals should converge with the data; this figure says they have.
The maximum shift in mean across the three priors, divided by the
median interval width, is zero to printed precision.}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Reading the results}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Why this null finding is informative}
A Bayesian project that matches a well-tuned classical baseline is
\emph{more} credible than one that claims a win.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \alert{Convergence is what the theory predicts.}
        Bernstein--von Mises says credible $\to$ confidence in regular
        parametric problems. We are in that regime ($n \approx 6500$,
        $p = 4$).
  \item \alert{Higher bar than most published claims.} The same null
        holds across asset (SPY $\to$ TLT), likelihood (Gaussian $\to$
        Student-$t$), cost (0.5$\times$, 1$\times$, 2$\times$), and
        prior strength.
  \item \alert{The sweep caught a real qualifier.} Tabular's win at
        \texttt{n\_bins=4} disappears at \texttt{n\_bins=2}; a
        single-config study would have missed this.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
\textbf{Bayesian Q-learning's empirical advantage is strongest in
regimes this project did not test} -- small-data, multi-asset
hierarchical, asymmetric-loss.
\note{This is the most important framing slide of the talk. Practice
saying ``a calibrated null is academically more credible than a clean
win'' until it sounds natural. The audience has heard a lot of papers
that beat a single baseline once; we are doing the opposite.}
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}{Why this \emph{is} Bayesian inference}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Parameters:} $\bm\beta_a$, $\bm\mu_\beta$,
        $\bm\Sigma_\beta$, $\sigma^2$ (+ $\lambda_t, \nu$ for the
        Student-$t$ branch).
  \item \textbf{Observations:} MC returns $y_1, \dots, y_n$,
        constructed deterministically from the data.
  \item \textbf{Posterior:}
        $p(\bm\beta_{1:|\A|}, \bm\mu_\beta, \bm\Sigma_\beta, \sigma^2
        \mid \D)$, sampled exactly by Gibbs.
  \item \textbf{Decision rule:} Thompson sampling --
        \alert{derived from the posterior}, not a heuristic.
  \item \textbf{Evaluation:} posterior-predictive distribution of every
        reported metric.
\end{itemize}

\medskip
RL enters only at the decision rule. Everything else is a hierarchical
Bayesian regression in the Gelman tradition.
\note{If the talk runs long, this is the one summary slide to keep.
Hit each line: parameters, observations, posterior, decision rule,
evaluation. ``At every step we used Bayes; the RL is the wrapping
paper.''}
\end{frame}

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================

\begin{frame}{Conclusion}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Built} a fully Bayesian Q-learning agent: hierarchical
        prior, conjugate Gibbs sampler, Student-$t$ extension via
        scale mixture, Thompson sampling decision rule, posterior-
        predictive evaluation throughout.
  \item \textbf{Found} a calibrated null on SPY: Bayesian Sharpe
        $-1.52$, 95\% CrI $[-2.58, -0.31]$, overlapping Linear FQI on
        every metric, across four robustness dimensions.
  \item \textbf{Validated} the calibration claim: the
        $\sigma^2$-prior sensitivity score is $0.000$ -- the
        intervals are data-dominated, not prior-driven.
  \item \textbf{Contributes} the framework -- explicit prior,
        likelihood, posterior, cadence, validity check -- rather than
        a treatment-effect win.
\end{itemize}

\bigskip
\textbf{Next steps:} hierarchical pooling \emph{across assets},
asymmetric-loss decision rules, Gaussian-process $Q$, TD-bootstrap
vs MC-supervised on the same fairness frame.
\note{The closing line: ``Bernstein--von Mises in the RL setting,
empirically demonstrated, with a framework that generalises to the
regimes where it matters more.'' Pause. Then ``Questions?''}
\end{frame}
